title: Arjuna asks which road
hookLine: Arjuna begs Krishna to name the one right way, and Krishna won't split them
carry: only the childish split the paths
tomorrow: guided visits: what a Sikh means by seva

cards: The battlefield of the Bhagavad Gita. Arjuna has heard Krishna praise two ways: giving up action to seek knowledge, and acting without craving for the fruit. He's confused, and he's honest about it.
At the start of the fifth chapter he says, in effect: you praise both. Tell me for certain which one is better. Just one.
It's the question anyone asks when a tradition offers too many doors: which is the real way?

teach.h: BOTH LEAD TO THE HIGHEST GOOD.
teach.b: Krishna's answer surprises him. Both lead to the highest good, he says, though of the two, acting without craving is the better.
Then comes the line Hindus still quote: it's the childish, not the wise, who speak of knowledge and action as separate. Settle into either one, and you reach what both reach.
Some teachers hear that as true of all three roads you've walked these three weeks.

teach.h: THE KITCHEN, THE SONG, THE QUESTION.
teach.b: The kitchen: the karma road ended with seva as a life, a king giving his last meal and asking nothing back. The song: the bhakti road ended with the Gita Govinda, God searching for the soul and, at the end, tending it.

The question: the jnana road ended with Ramana Maharshi on his hill, tracing each thought back to the Self. Hindus have argued for centuries about how these fit, and schools still disagree; this path doesn't settle it.

But look at many Hindu families and you'll see all three under one roof: a grandmother at the shrine before breakfast, a father who calls his volunteering seva, a teenager who sits quietly and asks who she is.
That isn't confusion. Many teachers would say it's what Krishna told Arjuna.

teach.h: KARMA: ALL THREE ARE A DOING.
teach.b: And notice the word under all three: karma, from a root meaning to do. The ladle is a doing. The song is a doing.
Even the question is a doing.

how: Hindus often speak of three great paths: karma (selfless action), bhakti (devotion) and jnana (knowledge). People often lean toward one, and some teachers say the paths meet; schools differ on how.

o: the silence that comes after the question
action, the doing under serving, singing, asking
a song sung only by temple dancers

games.q: each track and where it ended — tap the pairs.
p: which way is better? tell me one

s: this path ranks the three tracks, with knowledge as the advanced one
the tracks are electives, never ranked. Hindu teachers have long argued about how they fit; this path doesn't settle it.
in the Gita's fifth chapter, Krishna says knowledge and action lead to the same goal
both lead to the highest good; only the childish, not the wise, speak of them as separate (5.2–5).
Ramana Maharshi taught by asking people to answer 'who am I?' with their name
the opposite: not a name or a job. follow the thought 'I' back to its source and rest there.

games.q: someone asks you which of the three paths is the real one. what does the Gita's fifth chapter say?
o: knowledge is the real one; the others are warm-ups.
only the childish treat the ways as rivals.
action is the real one; the rest is talk.
games.why: the Gita (5.4) says it's the childish, not the wise, who speak of knowledge and action as separate; many teachers extend that to all three. Hindus still debate how the paths fit together.

practice: Let the track you walked come back to you: for the kitchen, one piece of work you did this month for someone else; for the song, a line or a name of God you love; for the question, let the word I rise and gently look for where it comes from.
If you pray, offer all three to God, as the Gita asks you to offer every action. No grade, no finish line.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action, from the Sanskrit root kri, to do. The first name on three tracks, and the ground under them all.

orig.note: Sanskrit karma, action, from the root kṛ, to do.

carryVoice: Your line: only the childish split the paths. Arjuna wanted one road; Krishna gave him the whole hill. Day three hundred twenty-two: three tracks, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.1–5 (Arjuna asks which is better; both lead to the highest good; the childish, not the wise, speak of sankhya and yoga as separate)
